cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-75-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits on a globe in the middle of the heavens among six angels, above a walled city with his tabernacle, 'his dwelling place in Sion'. People within the walls hold up offerings toward him, and outside a man points to his mouth with one hand and appeals to Christ with the other, the one who makes and pays his vow. The drawing illustrates the psalm of the God who 'is known in Judah'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-75-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-transfiguratio.summary: On a mountain of rounded hills Christ stands in white between Moses and Elijah, rays streaming down from above, while Peter, James and John fall to the ground at his feet. The gold background and the brilliant white of Christ's robe make the moment of revelation shine from the page.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
The Bayerische Staatsbibliothek has published the whole manuscript online with a Public Domain Mark, so every page can be studied in detail.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-transfiguratio.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 229); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:objects-leipzig-grassi-crucifixion-i.summary: Beneath an arch, Christ hangs on the cross with a large halo, his head bowed and his long body gently swaying; the Virgin raises her hand in grief at the left, while St John stands at the right, his hand to his cheek. The restrained composition gives the Crucifixion the stillness of an icon.
facts: Byzantine crucifixion ivories of the later 10th century often show Christ's body in a gentle curve with the head inclined in death, a type that spread to the West (type).

walters:71.377.summary: The Virgin stands in flowing drapery, holding the Christ Child upright on her left arm as he sits facing outward. Her right hand once held an object, perhaps a flower, now lost. The ivory statuette, mounted on a dark base, continues a conservative devotional type into the 18th century.
facts: The Walters describes the Virgin's features as French, while noting that the drapery has parallels in 17th-century works.
walters:71.377.notes: The worklist year (900) was wrong; the museum dates the figure to the 1st quarter of the 18th century. Image viewed on the Walters image server.
